questions.stem: At 18:55 the 27-month-old is alert, playing and drinking after a 3-minute febrile seizure. While you plan discharge, the frightened parent asks, "What do I do if it happens again?" What is the best first aid advice to give?
options: Lie them on their side, time it, nothing in mouth; call 000 if 5 min or more
Hold the limbs firmly, put a spoon between the teeth; call 000 if it lasts 10 minutes
Give paracetamol straight away, sponge with cool water; drive to ED if over 15 minutes
Sit them upright and give sips of water to stop choking; call 000 if the lips go dusky
questions.why: Seizure first aid is: note the time, recovery position, nothing in the mouth, don't restrain, stay with the child. Call an ambulance (000) if the seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, breathing is difficult or the child doesn't wake properly.
notes: Holding the limbs down can injure the child, putting objects in the mouth risks dental injury and aspiration, and 10 minutes is too long to wait before calling 000.
A seizing child can't swallow safely, cool sponging and antipyretics don't stop seizures, and waiting 15 minutes delays treatment of possible status epilepticus.
Giving fluids by mouth during or right after a seizure risks aspiration; the child should lie on their side, and the trigger to call 000 is a seizure lasting 5 minutes.

questions.stem: A 27-month-old (13 kg) had a single 3-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure with fever. Red throat, runny nose, normal ears, clear chest, no meningism or rash, BGL 5.6 mmol/L. Fifty minutes after the seizure the child has GCS 15 and is playing and drinking. What is the most appropriate approach to investigation?
options: No further tests; discharge once at baseline, with first aid teaching and GP follow-up
Catheter urine for microscopy and culture, then discharge with GP review of the result
FBC, electrolytes, calcium, glucose and blood culture, then discharge if all are normal
Outpatient EEG and MRI brain within 2 weeks to look for an underlying epileptic cause
questions.why: After a simple febrile seizure with a clear source and full recovery, no routine bloods, EEG or imaging are needed (RCH guideline). Look for the source of the fever, and send urine only if no source is found.
notes: Urine is collected for a fever with no source. This child has a clear viral URTI source.
Routine bloods do not change management after a simple febrile seizure in a well child who has fully recovered.
EEG and neuroimaging are not indicated after a simple febrile seizure and do not predict recurrence or later epilepsy.

questions.stem: The parent of a 27-month-old who has just had a simple febrile seizure during a viral URTI asks why fever causes fits in small children but not in adults. An older sibling had a febrile seizure at age 2. Which mechanism best explains febrile seizures in this age group?
options: Fever-induced cerebral oedema that raises intracranial pressure above a critical level
An immature brain with a low, often inherited, seizure threshold that fever lowers
Direct viral invasion of the cortex causing a brief, self-limiting viral encephalitis
Hypoglycaemia from poor intake, as young children have small hepatic glycogen stores
questions.why: The developing brain is more excitable and has a lower seizure threshold. Fever lowers that threshold further, and there is a strong genetic predisposition, which is why the risk falls away after about 6 years and runs in families.
notes: Fever doesn't cause meaningful cerebral oedema or raised ICP. A child with raised ICP would not be back to GCS 15 and playing within an hour.
Viral invasion of brain tissue is encephalitis, which causes ongoing drowsiness or focal signs, not full recovery within an hour.
Hypoglycaemia can cause seizures, but this child's BGL was 5.6 mmol/L and recovery happened without glucose.

questions.stem: Suppose this febrile 27-month-old had stayed drowsy with neck stiffness after the seizure. A lumbar puncture would then be needed to look for meningitis. With the child held in the lateral position, which interspace and landmark should you use?
options: T12/L1 interspace, at the level of the twelfth ribs and the lower thoracic spine
L1/L2 interspace, at the level of the lower costal margins in the midaxillary line
S1/S2 level, between the posterior superior iliac spines in the midline
L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace, at or just below the line joining the iliac crests
questions.why: By around age 2 the conus medullaris ends at about L1 to L2. A needle at L3/L4 or L4/L5, found at the line joining the iliac crests (Tuffier's line), enters the thecal sac below the cord.
notes: T12/L1 is at or above the conus medullaris, so a needle here risks injuring the spinal cord.
L1/L2 is about where the conus ends at this age, so it's too high to be safe. The costal margin isn't a reliable lumbar landmark.
The sacral vertebrae are fused, so there's no interspace to enter at S1/S2, and this is below the usual safe LP site.
